newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - AIDS cuts its way through S.African mines.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - AIDS cuts its way through S.African mines.

text.p: One worker dies of AIDS every day at one of the world's biggest mining corporations.
South Africa's Gencor Ltd estimates 20 percent of the 100,000-strong labour force at its coal, platinum and gold mines is infected by the HIV virus and 30 workers lose their lives to AIDS each month.

World AIDS Day, on Sunday, has again focused international eyes on Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS), the terminal disease that breaks down the body's ability to fight any illness, slowly and certainly killing its victims.
HIV is rampaging through South Africa with five million of the country's 40 million people likely to be infected by 2000, giving the country one of the world's fastest infection rates.
But the horror for South African health officials doesn't stop with HIV and AIDS.
They are struggling to fight another plague -- tuberculosis.

Unfurling rapidly throughout the country and becoming multi-drug resistant due to poor management of treatment and lack of international assistance during the apartheid years, TB is hitting the primitive rural areas hardest.
The country's vast mining industry says a sinister partnership exists between the two diseases.

"They've been called the cursed duet -- TB and HIV. The problem is that they are deleterious to each other. The HIV makes TB worse and TB makes HIV worse," Doctor Lettie La Grange of the Chamber of Mines, an employer association for the coal and gold mining industries.
"The mortality associated with cases who have TB with HIV is much higher and is the biggest cause of mortality in the industry," La Grange told Reuters.
It is said that a miner dies for every tonne of gold produced in South Africa, which turns out over 500 tonnes a year. But La Grange said disease was now overtaking accident as a killer.
"We're getting back to a situation (of 100 years ago) where our medical (disease) deaths will be more than our trauma-related deaths," he told Reuters.

Official estimates say two percent or one in 50 South African miners suffers from full-blown TB and one in seven is infected by the AIDS virus. Last year 30 percent of TB sufferers were also HIV-positive.

The "cursed duet" has infiltrated South Africa's largest employer, preying on an estimated 300,000-strong underground workforce. Thousands of metres underground, in sweltering temperatures, with little air and breathing fine dust, miners' lungs may deteriorate rapidly, making them prone to TB.

"We've got a workforce coming from the rural areas and many are already infected with TB. They're exposed to an environment which helps the bacillus become active. Miners are more prone to develop TB and HIV aggravates the situation," La Grange said.
There is a menacing corollary too.
Miners who are not infected by TB still risk contracting the AIDS virus, which smashes their immune system and leaves them exposed to an environment where they are likely to contract TB.
"It's quite obvious that our TB epidemic is related to HIV," La Grange said.
Mine doctors say that disease in the industry has spiralled out of control, exacting too high a price in lives, lost production, medical and education costs as well as death and sick benefits.

Assuming 15 percent of South African miners -- most numbers range between 10 and 20 percent -- are HIV-positive, the industry's overall productivity will drop by three to five percent next year, says Susan Foster, a lecturer in Health Economics at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine.

Already beleaguered by declining ore grades and some of the world's highest operating costs, South Africa's mines -- particularly gold mines which are eyeing their lowest output in 40 years -- cannot afford to lose either output or labour.
But the future seems to only hold gloom.

"It's very depressing. I'm already seeing it reflected in figures from our mines. We are starting to see the impact of the AIDS ill on health services and an increase in the number of actual deaths," said La Grange.
